title: Showing Others That You Have Heard Them
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Distinguishes listening from being heard, arguing leaders build outsized trust by explicitly summarizing what they've absorbed rather than simply nodding along. Walks through specific high-stakes moments where this pays off most -- responding to survey feedback, acknowledging a team member's risky candor, and de-escalating a charged emotional exchange. Provides a short list of stock phrases ('What I'm hearing is...', 'Let me make sure I've got this right...') that leaders can use to close the loop, arguing this closing act rewards honesty and increases future candor.
points: Explicitly summarizing what was heard, not just listening quietly, is what builds trust after survey feedback, risky candor, or a charged exchange.
A short set of stock phrases ('What I'm hearing is...', 'So, if I understand correctly...') gives leaders a reliable way to close the loop in the moment.
Being heard, on its own, often defuses conflict and satisfies people even before any action is taken.
quotes: People like it when leaders listen to them. But they like it even more when leaders “hear” them. The difference is in how leaders respond when they listen.
When a leader lets the team know publicly that they have heard the feedback and will reflect upon it, that builds trust and confidence.
By thanking them and saying, “Here is what I just heard you say,” leaders reward honesty and courage and project themselves to be malleable in their thinking.
Leaders who reflect what people are experiencing defuse conflict and encourage steadier emotions. Sometimes being heard is all that people need to feel satisfied.
The leader’s effort to close the loop between what they think they heard and the validation by others is rewarded by more openness and candidness in return.
